about.title: Dr. Abeer Alshammari
about.roleLine: Founder of CyberAbeer, GreenTrust AI, and CyberAbeer Labs
about.introParagraph1: Dr. Abeer Alshammari is a cybersecurity governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) practitioner with more than 20 years of experience building and maturing enterprise security programs.
about.introParagraph2: Her work spans cybersecurity policy and control frameworks, risk assessment across application, infrastructure, cloud, data, and third-party domains, and coordinating internal and external audits. She founded CyberAbeer to bring that same practitioner discipline to AI governance, through GreenTrust AI, and to security education, through CyberAbeer Labs.
about.introParagraph3: In parallel with her GRC leadership work, Dr. Abeer serves as a Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) and cybersecurity strategic consultant, advising organizations on security strategy, risk posture, and governance at the executive and board level. She works with leadership teams to turn cybersecurity risk into clear business decisions and practical maturity roadmaps.

governance.title: AI Governance Quick Check
governance.intro: Answer honestly for the most accurate result. This takes about two minutes.

questions.prompt: Does your organization maintain a complete inventory of AI agents in production?
Are AI agents formally risk-assessed before they go into production?
Is there a named owner accountable for each AI agent?
Do you review third-party AI tools for data access and risk before adoption?
Can you produce an audit trail of AI-related risk decisions if asked today?

governance.resultLow: Your AI governance practices appear to have significant gaps. Establishing an AI agent inventory is a strong first step.
governance.resultMedium: Your AI governance practices are developing. A few specific gaps are worth prioritizing.
governance.resultHigh: Your AI governance practices appear relatively mature. Formal audit-ready evidence is the natural next step.

quantum.title: Quantum Readiness Quick Check
quantum.intro: Answer honestly for the most accurate result. This takes about two minutes.

questions.prompt: Do you maintain an inventory of cryptographic algorithms in use across your systems?
Have you identified which systems rely on algorithms considered vulnerable to future quantum attacks?
Do you have a migration plan toward post-quantum cryptographic algorithms?
Do you know which of your long-lived sensitive data could be at risk from harvest-now, decrypt-later attacks?
Is a specific person or team accountable for quantum readiness?

quantum.resultLow: Quantum readiness work has likely not started yet. Beginning with a cryptographic asset inventory is a practical first step.
quantum.resultMedium: Quantum readiness work is underway. A documented migration plan is a reasonable next step.
quantum.resultHigh: Quantum readiness practices appear relatively mature for this early stage of the industry.

greentrustAssessment.title: GreenTrust AI Agent Governance Assessment
greentrustAssessment.intro: Sixteen quick questions across eight governance domains. No confidential company information is required, and this assessment does not use AI to score your answers: every result is calculated with a fixed, disclosed scoring method, not a language model.

visibility.name: AI Agent Visibility
visibility.recommendation: Start with a simple, living inventory of every AI agent, bot, and autonomous tool in use, including ones adopted informally by individual teams.

accountability.name: Ownership & Accountability
accountability.recommendation: Assign a named, accountable owner to every AI agent before it goes into production, not after something goes wrong.

identity.name: Agent Identity
identity.recommendation: Give every agent its own scoped identity and credentials, separate from any human user's login, with a defined rotation schedule.

permissions.name: Permissions
permissions.recommendation: Move agents toward least-privilege access scoped to the specific task, and keep a reliable, current record of what each agent can reach.

oversight.name: Human Oversight
oversight.recommendation: Require human approval before high-impact actions, and make sure a tested override or kill-switch exists for every agent.

monitoring.name: Logging & Monitoring
monitoring.recommendation: Centralize agent activity logging and put a regular, defined cadence in place for someone to actually review it.

lifecycle.name: Lifecycle Governance
lifecycle.recommendation: Document a decommissioning process, including access revocation, and put agents on a periodic review cycle as their role or data access changes.

shadowAi.name: Shadow AI
shadowAi.recommendation: Make the approved path to adopting an AI tool easy enough that teams use it, and build a no-blame process to bring existing shadow AI under governance.

questions.prompt: Does your organization maintain an inventory of every AI agent, bot, or autonomous tool in use?
options: Yes, a maintained and regularly updated inventory
We have a partial or outdated list

questions.prompt: When a team adopts a new AI tool or agent, how does your organization find out?
options: A required registration or approval step before use

We typically don't find out until something goes wrong

questions.prompt: Does each AI agent have a named, accountable human owner?
options: Yes, every agent has a named owner

questions.prompt: If an AI agent takes a harmful or incorrect action, is it clear who is accountable for the outcome?
options: Yes, accountability is clearly defined in advance
It would take investigation to figure out

questions.prompt: Do AI agents use their own distinct credentials, separate from any human user's login?
options: Yes, every agent has its own scoped identity
Some agents share credentials with humans or each other
Agents mostly reuse existing human or service accounts

questions.prompt: Are agent credentials rotated, expired, or revoked on a defined schedule?
options: Only when we remember or something breaks

questions.prompt: Do AI agents operate under least-privilege access, scoped only to what each task requires?
options: Yes, permissions are scoped per task and agent
Permissions are broader than necessary in places
Agents generally have broad, standing access

questions.prompt: Can you produce, today, a list of every system and dataset a given AI agent can access?
For high-impact actions (financial, customer-facing, irreversible), is a human required to approve before the agent proceeds?
If an agent behaves unexpectedly, is there a fast, well-understood way for a human to pause or override it?
options: Yes, a tested override or kill-switch process

questions.prompt: Are AI agent actions logged in a way that supports after-the-fact review?
Does anyone regularly review agent activity logs for anomalies or policy violations?
options: Yes, on a regular defined cadence

questions.prompt: Is there a defined process for retiring or updating an AI agent, including revoking its access?
options: No process; agents are abandoned in place

questions.prompt: Are AI agents periodically reassessed as their role, data access, or capability changes?
options: Yes, on a scheduled review cycle
Only when a problem forces a review
Agents are set up once and never revisited

questions.prompt: Do employees or teams sometimes adopt AI tools or agents without an IT or security review?
options: Rarely; there's a clear, easy approved path
Sometimes, and we know it happens
Frequently, and we don't have visibility into it

questions.prompt: If shadow AI use is discovered, is there a defined process to bring it under governance rather than simply banning or ignoring it?
options: Yes, a clear onboarding and remediation path

firstDefender.badgeDescription: Awarded for completing the First Defender: Spot the Phish challenge.
firstDefender.heroSubtitle: Five realistic messages just landed. Inspect each one like a real analyst would, decide what to do, and earn your first badge, free, no signup required to start.
firstDefender.missionBody: It is your first day on the security team at Nova Retail, a fictional company built just for this challenge. Five messages arrive today: emails and one text message. Tap to inspect each one, then choose what you would actually do.
firstDefender.phishedLabel: In this simulation, that would have gotten you phished

step1.subject: Your password expires in 2 hours, action required
step1.preview: Your account will be locked if you do not update your password immediately using the secure link below.
step1.senderRevealed: it-support@nova-retai1.com, the domain replaces the letter L with the number 1
step1.toneRevealed: Urgency language: "expires in 2 hours", "will be locked", "immediately"
step1.hint: Check the sender's domain very carefully, letter by letter.
step1.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Reporting it protects your whole team, since attackers usually send the same message to many people at once.
step1.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite. Look again at the sender's domain name.
step1.feedbackPhished: Clicking would have sent your real password to an attacker. In this simulation, that is exactly what a lookalike domain like this one is built to do.
step1.explanation: The domain "nova-retai1.com" swaps the letter L for the number 1, a classic lookalike domain. Legitimate IT teams do not create true emergencies out of routine password resets. Urgency plus a lookalike domain is one of the most common phishing patterns there is.

step2.subject: Shared file with you: Q3 budget.xlsx
step2.preview: Hi, I shared the Q3 budget file with you. Click below to view it.
step2.linkRevealed: Real destination: http://drive-nova-files.co/login, not your organization's real file-sharing domain
step2.toneRevealed: Casual, friendly tone, no urgency, which is exactly why the link deserves a closer look rather than instant trust
step2.hint: The sender looks real. Check where the link actually goes before deciding.
step2.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The sender's name looks legitimate, but names are easy to spoof or copy. Confirming with Sara directly, through a number or chat you already had, is the safer move before entering any credentials.
step2.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite. The sender's email looks fine, so look at where the link itself actually leads.
step2.feedbackPhished: The link leads to a fake login page designed to capture whatever you type into it. In this simulation, that would have handed over your real password.
step2.explanation: The sender's name and address look legitimate, but the link goes to "drive-nova-files.co", not your organization's real file-sharing domain. Attackers often impersonate a real colleague's name. Before entering credentials anywhere, verify through a channel you already trust, like a phone number you already had, not one supplied in the message itself.

step3.fromAddress: Unknown number, not saved in your contacts
step3.preview: I'm in a meeting and can't talk. I need you to buy 5 gift cards for a client gift, $100 each. Send me the codes now, I'll pay you back. Please keep this between us for now.
step3.senderRevealed: This number has never contacted you before, and it does not match any saved number for your CEO.
step3.toneRevealed: Urgency ("now"), unusual request (personal gift cards), and secrecy ("keep this between us") together are a major warning sign
step3.hint: Real executives don't ask you to keep financial requests secret.
step3.feedbackCorrect: Correct. This is a textbook CEO fraud pattern, adapted to text messages. Reporting it and verifying separately protects you and anyone else who might receive the same message.
step3.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite. Look again at the number this came from, and how the message asks you to keep it quiet.
step3.feedbackPhished: In this simulation, buying and sending the gift card codes would have handed real money straight to an attacker, with no way to get it back.
step3.explanation: This is a classic CEO fraud, or business email compromise, adapted to text messages. Urgency, an unusual financial request, an unfamiliar number, and a request for secrecy together are major warning signs. Never send money or gift card codes based on a single message, no matter who it claims to be from.

step4.subject: Invoice #88213 overdue, see attachment
step4.preview: Please find your overdue invoice attached. Open immediately to avoid service suspension.
step4.senderRevealed: billing@quickinvoice-pay.net has no connection to your organization or any vendor you recognize.
step4.toneRevealed: Urgency ("avoid service suspension") paired with an unfamiliar sender and an unexpected attachment
step4.attachmentRevealed: Invoice_88213.zip is a compressed file. Compressing an attachment is a common way to slip past basic antivirus scanning.
step4.hint: You don't recognize this sender or this invoice. Compressed attachments from strangers are risky.
step4.feedbackCorrect: Correct. You have no relationship with this sender or this invoice, and the attachment is a compressed file, a common way to hide malware from basic scanners.
step4.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite. You don't recognize this sender. Consider what opening an unexpected attachment from a stranger could do.
step4.feedbackPhished: In this simulation, opening that attachment would have installed malware on your device.
step4.explanation: You don't have an existing relationship with this sender or this invoice, and the attachment is a compressed .zip file, a common way to hide malware from basic email scanners. Unexpected attachments from unknown senders should be reported, not opened, even when the subject line creates urgency.

step5.subject: This month at Nova Retail: new parking policy and team updates
step5.preview: Read about the new parking arrangement starting next month and other team news.
step5.senderRevealed: newsletter@nova-retail.com, matches your organization's real domain
step5.toneRevealed: Calm, informational tone. No urgency, no request for money, credentials, or any action at all
step5.hint: Check whether anything here asks you to click, pay, or share information under pressure.
step5.feedbackCorrect: Correct. A matching company domain, no urgency, and no request for money, credentials, or sensitive action. Recognizing safe messages is just as important a skill as spotting dangerous ones.
step5.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite. Look again: does anything here actually ask you to click, pay, or share information?
step5.feedbackPhished: This message never asked you to do anything risky, so nothing happens in this simulation, but it's worth noticing that reporting or ignoring genuine mail as a reflex can create alert fatigue on a real team.
step5.explanation: This is a normal internal newsletter: a matching company domain, no urgency, and no request for money, credentials, or sensitive action. Reporting genuine messages as phishing creates alert fatigue and makes real reports harder for a security team to act on quickly.
